strings: Solve mysteries with tables, charts and claims!
Pro cases: chapters 4 to 7. Chapter 1 is a warm-up.
Explorer cases: chapters 1 to 3 and My Data.
Is this claim supported by the chart?
Row: {name}. What should happen to it?
Fix, merge, remove, or keep it as it is.
Show me! Tap the evidence that proves it.
Show me first: get the view that answers the question on screen, then pin your claim.
The view supports a claim. Pin one!
Show me: the claim card opens when the view on screen answers the question.
Not that one. Which row or bar shows it?
Yes! Keep going: tap the rest of the evidence.
Good claim! Now show me: tap the evidence that proves it.
Skipped. No stars this time, but the next case is open.
That view answers it. Pin your claim!
Think about what the data showed you.
Your work is saved. You can go back to your class page now.
Four digits from your teacher: chapter, band, mode, case.
That is not a case. Check the four digits with your teacher.
A lunchbox went missing from the hall after lunch. Here is who was where, and when.
Who was last in the hall?
Sorted by When, the last Hall row is Gus at 3:10. Jo was later, but in the Yard.
A table holds facts in rows and columns. Sorting puts the rows in order, and grouping counts how many of each kind. The right view makes the answer pop out.
Which column would tell us when each kid was there?
The When column is glowing. Tap its header to sort by time.
I sorted the table by When for you. Now read the Hall rows from the bottom.
What does sorting a table do?
Four teams built block towers. The judge lost the ribbon!
Which team built the tallest tower?
Sorted by Blocks, the biggest number is 21, and that row is the Foxes.
Which column holds the height of each tower?
Blocks is glowing. Tap it to sort by height.
Sorted by Blocks for you. The biggest number is at one end.
To find the biggest number fast, you should…
Every kid in the class drew their pet. Dot wants one number: which pet wins?
Which pet is most common in the class?
Grouped by Pet, the Dog bar is the tallest: 4 kids.
Sorting lists every row. Group puts the rows with the same value together and counts them, so you see how many of each kind.
Sorting lists every row. What would count the pets instead?
The Group button is glowing. Group by Pet to count each kind.
I grouped the rows by Pet for you. Read the counts.
The library keeps a visitor list. Which day needs an extra helper?
On which day did the most kids visit?
Grouped by Day, Tuesday has the most visits: 3.
Do you need the names, or how many per day?
Group is glowing. Group by Day.
Grouped by Day for you. Which bar is tallest?
Which view answers “how many per day?” fastest?
Sports day! Everyone ran one lap. One column is just for fun.
Sorted by Seconds, the smallest number is 45, and that is Uma. Shoes do not matter here.
Fastest means the fewest seconds. Which column has seconds?
Sorted by Seconds for you. Fastest is the smallest number.
The class voted for a party snack. Dot wants to know what to skip.
Which snack did the fewest kids pick?
Grouped by Snack, Crackers has the shortest bar: 1 vote.
Fewest means the smallest count. How do you get counts?
Grouped for you. Look for the shortest bar.
The shortest bar in a group count means…
The lunch helper counted fruit picks. Pick the view that shows the winner at a glance.
The bar chart shows Grape with the tallest bar: 7.
A bar chart turns counts into bars, so the biggest and smallest jump out. A pictograph uses pictures. A table keeps every exact fact.
Which view shows big and small at a glance?
Switched to bars for you. The tallest bar wins.
A bar chart is best for…
Dot has the pet counts in a table but the chart is empty. Build it!
Make the bars match the table. Then: which pet is most common?
When the bars match the table, Dog is the tallest: 5.
Each bar should be as tall as its number in the table.
The Dog stepper is glowing: tap + until Dog shows 5.
I set Dog to 5 for you. Match the other three.
The sports club made a pictograph. Each picture stands for 2 kids.
How many more kids chose Soccer than Swimming?
Soccer has 8 and Swimming has 4. 8 minus 4 is 4.
Which view shows the two amounts side by side? Each picture is 2 kids.
Switched to pictures for you. Soccer 8, Swimming 4: take the smaller from the bigger.
In this pictograph one picture means…
A chart is great for amounts, but someone has a question only a table can answer.
Only the table keeps the names. Nia’s row says Grape.
Does a bar chart show names?
Switched to the table for you. Find the Grape row.
Color vote! Build the bars and spot the color nobody chose.
With the bars built, Green stays at 0: nobody picked it.
Build each bar to its number. One of them stays flat.
Green is glowing. Its number is 0.
I built Red to 3 for you. Finish the rest, then find the flat bar.
Dot measured a bean plant every day for five days.
The plant grows about 2 cm a day.
Each bar is 2 cm taller than the one before: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That supports the claim.
A claim is something you say is true. The chart is the evidence. It can support the claim, go against it, or be too small to tell yet.
How much does each bar grow from one day to the next?
Day 2 and Day 3 are glowing. Compare their heights.
4 to 6 is 2 more. Every day adds 2. The claim is supported.
The caretaker counted bikes at the rack every morning this week.
Friday is the busiest bike day.
Thursday’s bar is the tallest: 15. Friday has 13. The chart goes against the claim.
Thursday is glowing. Compare it with Friday.
Thursday 15 is more than Friday 13, so the claim is not supported.
The chart says Thursday 15 and Friday 13. “Friday is busiest” is…
A sunflower was measured on two days. Someone is already making a big prediction.
It will be 20 cm tall by day 10.
Two bars is a hunch, not a case. We need more days before we can tell.
How many days of data do we have?
Both bars are glowing. Is that enough to see a pattern?
Two points can make any line. Pick Can’t tell yet.
Dot says: two clues is a hunch, five is a…
Back to the bean plant. Five days are in. What will day 6 measure?
Slide to your prediction for day 6, then pin it.
The plant adds 2 cm a day: 10 on day 5, so day 6 should be about 12.
What is the step from one day to the next?
Day 4 and Day 5 are glowing: 8 then 10.
A prediction from a steady pattern is…
A class list has shoe sizes and books read this month. Someone sees a link.
Kids with bigger shoes read more books.
Bo has size 3 and read 1 book; Cy has size 2 and read 6. Bigger shoes do not mean more books.
Does the Books column go up when Shoe size goes up?
Bo and Cy are glowing. Compare their two numbers.
Size 3 read 1, size 2 read 6. No pattern: not supported.
Do not have to be connected
Sports day again. The list has hair color and laps run. A new claim is on the board.
The smallest number in Laps is 3, so everyone ran at least 3. Hair color does not come into it.
What is the smallest number in the Laps column?
Ida and Kai are glowing: the smallest laps.
The smallest is 3, which is at least 3. Supported.
Twelve kids typed their pet. Some typed in a hurry. Clean the list before counting.
How many kids have a dog?
After fixing the three misspelled dogs, the Dog group counts 7.
Real data has typos, double entries and impossible numbers. Clean it first: fix a typo, merge a duplicate, remove what cannot be true. Then count.
Some rows say the same pet in a different way. Can you spot them?
The odd rows are glowing. Tap one and fix its spelling.
I fixed Cy’s row to Dog. Fix the other two, then group by Pet.
The sign-up sheet was passed round twice. Some kids are on it two times.
Which club has the most kids?
Once Ori and Sol are counted once each, Art has 3 and Chess has 2.
Is anyone on the list twice?
The repeated rows are glowing. Tap one and merge it.
I merged Ori’s second row. Merge Sol’s, then group by Club.
Kids typed their age for the reading club. Two numbers cannot be true.
What is the most common age?
99 and 1 cannot be club ages. Without them, age 10 is the biggest group: 4 kids.
Which ages could not be a kid in this club?
Two rows are glowing. Tap one and remove it.
I removed the 99. Remove the other impossible age, then group by Age.
An age of 99 in a kids’ club list is…
A typo for 9 that you keep
Sports club sign-ups: typos, a double entry and an impossible number, all in one list.
Which sport has the most kids?
Clean, the list has 4 Tennis kids, 3 Soccer and 2 Swimming.
Look for three kinds of mess: spelling, a repeat, an impossible number.
The messy rows are glowing. Fix, merge or remove each one.
I fixed Lu’s row. Do the other three, then group by Sport.
Which fix is right for an age of 120?
Two classes counted who walks to school. Class B has more walkers, but it is a bigger class.
Which class has the bigger share of walkers?
As a share, Class A is 50% and Class B is 40%. More walkers, but a smaller share.
To compare groups of different sizes, turn counts into percent: part divided by whole, times 100. Then every group is out of 100.
12 is more than 10, but the classes are different sizes. What would make them fair to compare?
Switched to percent for you: A 50%, B 40%.
To compare groups of different sizes
Three classes sent their recycling counts. One row cannot be right. Fix the list, then compare shares.
Which class recycled the biggest share of its lunches?
Class C says 30 of 20, which cannot be. Without it: A 75%, B 80%.
One class recycled more lunches than it had. Which one?
Class C is glowing. Remove it, then use %.
I removed Class C. Now tap % to compare shares.
